title: INNER JOIN
objective: Combine two tables with INNER JOIN, keep only matching rows, and know exactly which rows an INNER JOIN throws away.
context: Most reporting joins are INNER JOINs: order lines with product names, products with supplier details. They are correct when — and only when — an unmatched row is genuinely irrelevant to the question. The merchandising team needs several of these lookups this week.

exercises.title: Product catalogue with supplier
exercises.question: Merchandising wants each product listed with the supplier who provides it.
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, product_name, supplier_name and supplier_country (suppliers.country) for every product that has a matching supplier.
hints: Driving table is products; supplier details are looked up.
'that has a matching supplier' → unmatched products can go → INNER JOIN.
FROM products p JOIN suppliers s ON s.supplier_id = p.supplier_id, alias s.country AS supplier_country
exercises.why: Enriching a fact/child table with dimension attributes is everyday SQL — and you must know which rows the INNER JOIN filtered out before you call the list 'complete'.

recall.q: Which rows does an INNER JOIN drop?
recall.a: Rows on either side with no match on the join condition — including rows whose key is NULL.

exercises.join_notes: products 25 rows, suppliers 5. Result: 23 rows. Products→supplier is many-to-one, so nothing multiplies. Two products silently disappear: product 21 'Water Bottle' (supplier_id 9 does not exist) and product 22 'Phone Stand' (supplier_id NULL). Supplier 5 'Andes Trading' also never appears — it has no products, so its NULL country never shows up either. The result contains no NULLs at all — INNER JOIN output never has join-generated NULLs.

exercises.title: Order lines with product names
exercises.question: The warehouse team wants a readable picking list: every order line with the product name and category.
exercises.prompt: Return order_item_id, order_id, product_name, category, quantity and line_total (quantity * unit_price from order_items) for all order lines.
hints: Driving table = order_items (one row per line). Products is the lookup.
Use oi.unit_price, not p.list_price, for line_total.
FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
exercises.why: Line-level detail with descriptive attributes is the base layer of almost every sales report.

recall.q: Which table's grain does this result have?
recall.a: order_items — one row per order line.

exercises.join_notes: order_items 150 rows, products 25. Result: 150 rows — every line's product_id exists in products, so INNER drops no lines and nothing multiplies (product_id is products' primary key). Seen from the products side the relationship is one-to-many: product 9 appears on 15 lines. Products 23, 24 and 25 were never sold and do not appear. category is NULL on the 13 lines of product 20 — that NULL comes from the data, not from the join.

exercises.title: 2025 orders with customer names — what went missing?
exercises.question: Account managers want every order placed in 2025 with the customer's name.
exercises.prompt: Using an INNER JOIN, return order_id, order_date, customer_name (customers.name) and order_status for orders with order_date on or after '2025-01-01'. (Then compare your row count with the number of 2025 orders.)
hints: Filter on o.order_date >= '2025-01-01' (compare with a full date string).
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.order_date >= '2025-01-01'
exercises.why: This is how revenue goes missing in real dashboards: an INNER JOIN to a dimension with a gap drops facts without any error. Always reconcile the joined count with the base count.

recall.q: You INNER JOIN orders to customers and get fewer rows than there are orders. What happened?
recall.a: Some orders have a customer_id with no match (orphan or NULL key) — INNER JOIN dropped them.

exercises.join_notes: There are 30 orders dated 2025 (orders 31–60), but the result has only 29 rows. Order 31 (2025-01-08, completed) has customer_id 99, which is not in customers, so the INNER JOIN silently removed it — a completed order worth 363.30 vanishes from the report. Each order matches at most one customer, so there is no multiplication; customers with several 2025 orders (customer 14 has 4) simply repeat.

exercises.title: Customers and orders by region
exercises.question: Regional managers want to know, per region, how many distinct customers have ordered and how many orders they placed.
exercises.prompt: Return region, customers_with_orders (count of distinct customers who placed at least one order) and order_count (number of orders, any status), one row per region (NULL region is its own group). Only orders that match an existing customer count.
hints: After joining, each customer appears once per order — so counting customers needs DISTINCT.
GROUP BY c.region; NULL regions form one group automatically.
SELECT c.region, COUNT(DISTINCT c.customer_id) AS customers_with_orders, COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON ... GROUP BY c.region
exercises.why: One-to-many joins inflate counts of the 'one' side. COUNT(DISTINCT parent_key) is the standard defence.

recall.q: After joining customers to orders, why COUNT(DISTINCT c.customer_id)?
recall.a: Each customer row is repeated once per order; plain COUNT would count orders, not customers.

exercises.join_notes: customers 20, orders 60 → 59 joined rows (order 31's customer 99 does not exist). Customers are multiplied by their orders: West has 4 customers but 17 joined rows. Result: 5 groups — East 4/14, North 3/13, South 4/11, West 4/17 and a NULL-region group 2/4 (customers 9 and 16). That NULL comes from the customers data, not from the join. Total customers_with_orders = 17; customers 18, 19, 20 have no orders and are dropped by the INNER JOIN.

exercises.title: Deeply discounted order lines
exercises.question: Pricing wants every order line sold at least 15% below the catalogue list price.
exercises.prompt: Return order_item_id, product_name, list_price, unit_price and discount_pct = 100.0 * (list_price - unit_price) / list_price rounded to 1 decimal, for lines whose ROUNDED discount_pct is at least 15 (round before comparing — floating-point division gives values like 14.9999…).
hints: list_price lives in products; unit_price in order_items.
You can't use the alias discount_pct in WHERE — repeat the rounded expression there.
exercises.why: Comparing what was charged (fact) to a reference value (dimension) is impossible without a join — and NULL reference values silently fall out of the comparison.

recall.q: Product 19 has a NULL list_price. Do its lines appear in this result?
recall.a: No — the discount expression is NULL, and NULL >= 15 is not true, so WHERE drops them.

exercises.join_notes: The join itself keeps all 150 lines (each line has exactly one product). Of those, 78 were sold at list price, 26 at a 10% discount, 36 at a 15% discount, and 10 (product 19 'Adjustable Dumbbells') have a NULL list_price, so their discount is NULL and they cannot pass the filter. Result: 36 rows (without ROUND in WHERE, float noise like 14.99999 would wrongly drop 11 of them). Here the rows disappear because of WHERE + NULL, not because of the join — learn to tell the two apart.

exercises.title: Self-join: possible duplicate customers
exercises.question: The CRM team suspects duplicate customer records whose names differ only by upper/lower case.
exercises.prompt: Join customers to itself and return customer_id_1, name_1, customer_id_2, name_2 for every pair of different customers whose names are equal ignoring case (LOWER), listing each pair once with customer_id_1 < customer_id_2.
hints: A self-join uses the same table twice with two different aliases.
Put a.customer_id < b.customer_id in the ON clause to avoid self-pairs and mirror duplicates.
FROM customers a JOIN customers b ON LOWER(a.name) = LOWER(b.name) AND a.customer_id < b.customer_id
exercises.why: Self-joins compare rows within one table: duplicates, hierarchies (manager → employee), consecutive events.

recall.q: Why a.customer_id < b.customer_id instead of a.customer_id <> b.customer_id?
recall.a: <> returns each pair twice (1,19) and (19,1); < returns each pair once.

exercises.join_notes: customers (20 rows) joined to itself. Without the id condition every customer matches at least itself (20 self-pairs) and the duplicates match each other in both directions. With a.customer_id < b.customer_id we keep 2 rows: (1 'Alice Johnson', 19 'alice johnson') and (3 'John Smith', 4 'John Smith'). Customer 5 'Jon Smith' is not matched — LOWER() fixes case, not spelling. Every other customer has no partner and is dropped by the INNER JOIN.

worked_example.question: Show order lines of order 2 with the product name.
worked_example.sql:
SELECT oi.order_item_id,
       oi.order_id,
       p.product_name,
       oi.quantity,
       oi.unit_price
FROM order_items AS oi
JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE oi.order_id = 2;
worked_example.explanation: Driving table: order_items (one row per line). Each line has exactly one product, so the row count equals the number of lines of order 2. INNER is safe here: every product_id in order_items exists in products.

recipe:
**The join recipe — do it in this order, every time, before typing SQL**

1. **Pick the driving table.** Which table's rows is the answer *about*? ("every customer…", "each order line…")
   That table goes first, after `FROM` — it is the **left table**.
2. **Name the right table(s) and the shared key.** What column links them? Is it PK → FK (one-to-many) or
   one-to-one? Which side is the "many" side?
3. **Ask: "must every row of the left table survive, even with no match?"**
   - no → `INNER JOIN` (unmatched rows silently disappear)
   - yes → `LEFT JOIN` (unmatched rows stay, right-side columns become NULL)
   - rows from *both* sides must survive → `FULL OUTER JOIN`
4. **Predict the row count before you run it.** Count the inputs (`SELECT COUNT(*) …`), think about
   matches per row (0, 1 or many), write your guess down — then run and compare. A surprise means
   you misunderstood the grain, the key or the data.

**INNER JOIN = intersection on the key.** A row appears only if the ON condition is true for some row on the
other side. Unmatched rows on *either* side vanish — **silently**, with no warning.

```sql
SELECT p.product_name, s.supplier_name
FROM   products  AS p                          -- 1. driving table
INNER JOIN suppliers AS s                      -- 2. right table
        ON s.supplier_id = p.supplier_id;      -- 2. shared key
-- 3. must every product survive? no → INNER
-- 4. predict: 25 products, 2 have no valid supplier → 23 rows
```

- `JOIN` alone means `INNER JOIN`.
- Always qualify columns (`p.`, `s.`) — both tables may have a column with the same name.
- Row count rule: each left row appears once **per matching right row** (0, 1 or many times).
- The ON clause can be any condition — not only equality (self-join with `<`, ranges, `lower(a)=lower(b)`).
common_mistakes: Assuming an INNER JOIN result is 'all the orders' — it silently drops any row whose key has no match (order 31!).
Forgetting that NULL keys never match, so rows with a NULL FK disappear from an INNER JOIN.
Counting the 'one' side after a one-to-many join without DISTINCT, inflating customer counts.
Writing ambiguous column names (e.g. supplier_id) without a table alias when both tables have the column.
Using products.list_price as revenue instead of order_items.unit_price.
recall: What does JOIN without a keyword mean?
How many times does a left row appear in an INNER JOIN?
Once per matching right row — 0, 1 or many.
How can you detect that an INNER JOIN dropped rows?
Compare COUNT(*) of the driving table (with the same filters) to the joined count, or run the anti-join.
review_next: Lesson 11: LEFT JOIN — keep every row of the driving table, even when it has no match. You'll bring back order 31, customers 18–20 and products 21–22 that INNER JOIN dropped here.
